verses.text: This is where the good news about Jesus Christ, God’s Son, begins.
As the prophets wrote: “Look, I’m sending my messenger ahead of you; he’ll prepare your way.
He’s a voice calling out in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the Lord’s way! Make his paths straight!’”
John appeared in the wilderness, baptizing and preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins.
People from the whole Judean countryside and Jerusalem came out to him. As they confessed their sins, John baptized them in the Jordan River.
John wore clothes made of camel hair with a leather belt around his waist. He ate locusts and wild honey.
He preached, “Someone stronger than me is coming after me. I’m not even worthy to bend down and untie his sandal straps.
I baptized you with water, but he’ll baptize you with the Holy Spirit.”
Around that time, Jesus came from Nazareth in Galilee, and John baptized him in the Jordan.
As Jesus came up out of the water, he saw the heavens split open and the Spirit coming down on him like a dove.
A voice came from heaven: “You are my beloved Son. I’m pleased with you.”
Right away, the Spirit sent him out into the wilderness.
He was there for forty days, tempted by Satan. He was with the wild animals, and angels took care of him.
After John was arrested, Jesus went into Galilee, announcing God’s good news.
He said, “The time has come! God’s kingdom is near. Turn back and believe the good news.”
As Jesus walked beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and his brother Andrew throwing a net into the water. They were fishermen.
Jesus said, “Come follow me, and I’ll teach you to fish for people.”
They immediately left their nets and followed him.
A little farther along, he saw James son of Zebedee and his brother John. They were in a boat mending their nets.
He called them, and they left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired workers and followed him.
They went to Capernaum. On the Sabbath, Jesus went into the synagogue and began teaching.
People were amazed at his teaching, because he taught with authority, unlike the legal experts.
Just then, a man with an impure spirit was in their synagogue, and he shouted,
“What do you want with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God!”
Jesus ordered him, “Be quiet! Come out of him!”
The impure spirit shook the man violently, cried out, and came out of him.
Everyone was stunned and asked each other, “What’s this? A new teaching—and with authority! He even commands impure spirits, and they obey him!”
News about Jesus quickly spread throughout the whole region of Galilee.
As soon as they left the synagogue, they went with James and John to the home of Simon and Andrew.
Simon’s mother-in-law was in bed with a fever, and they told Jesus about her right away.
He went to her, took her hand, and helped her up. The fever left her, and she began serving them.
That evening after sunset, people brought Jesus everyone who was sick or possessed by demons.
The whole town gathered at the door.
Jesus healed many people with all kinds of diseases and drove out many demons. He wouldn’t let the demons speak, because they knew who he was.
Very early the next morning, while it was still dark, Jesus got up, went outside, and headed to a quiet place to pray.
Simon and the others went searching for him.
When they found him, they said, “Everyone’s looking for you.”
He replied, “Let’s go to the nearby towns so I can preach there too. That’s why I came.”
He traveled throughout Galilee, preaching in their synagogues and driving out demons.
A man with a skin disease came to Jesus. He begged him, knelt down, and said, “If you’re willing, you can make me clean.”
Jesus was moved with compassion. He reached out, touched him, and said, “I am willing. Be clean!”
Immediately the disease left him, and he was clean.
Jesus sent him away at once, sternly warning him,
“Don’t tell anyone. Go show yourself to the priest, and bring the offering Moses commanded for your cleansing as a testimony to them.”

But the man went out and started telling everyone what happened, spreading the news everywhere. As a result, Jesus could no longer enter a town openly. He stayed outside in quiet places, but people came to him from all over.
A few days later, Jesus returned to Capernaum. Word got around that he was home,
and so many people gathered that there wasn’t room even outside the door. He was sharing God’s message with them.
Some people came, carrying a paralyzed man. Four of them were carrying him.
They couldn’t get him to Jesus because of the crowd, so they opened the roof above Jesus. After digging through it, they lowered the mat the paralyzed man was lying on.
When Jesus saw their faith, he said to the man, “Child, your sins are forgiven.”
Some legal experts were sitting there, thinking to themselves,
“Why is he talking like this? That’s blasphemy! Who can forgive sins except God alone?”
Jesus immediately knew in his spirit what they were thinking, so he said, “Why are you thinking this in your hearts?
Which is easier: to tell this paralyzed man, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Get up, pick up your mat, and walk’?
But I want you to know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins.” Then he said to the paralyzed man,
“I’m telling you, get up, pick up your mat, and go home.”
The man got up, picked up his mat, and walked out in front of everyone. They were all amazed and praised God, saying, “We’ve never seen anything like this!”
Jesus went out again beside the lake. The crowd came to him, and he taught them.
As he walked along, he saw Levi son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth. Jesus said to him, “Follow me.” Levi got up and followed him.
Later, Jesus was eating at Levi’s house. Many tax collectors and sinners were eating with him and his disciples, because many of them were following him.
When the legal experts from the Pharisees saw Jesus eating with sinners and tax collectors, they asked his disciples, “Why does he eat with tax collectors and sinners?”
Jesus heard them and said, “Healthy people don’t need a doctor; sick people do. I didn’t come to call righteous people, but sinners.”
John’s disciples and the Pharisees were fasting. Some people came and asked Jesus, “Why do John’s disciples and the Pharisees’ disciples fast, but yours don’t?”
Jesus answered, “Can wedding guests fast while the groom is with them? As long as they have the groom with them, they can’t fast.
But the time will come when the groom is taken away from them. On that day, they’ll fast.
No one patches an old coat with unshrunk cloth. Otherwise, the patch pulls away from it, new from old, and the tear gets worse.
And no one pours new wine into old wineskins. Otherwise, the wine will burst the skins, and both the wine and the skins will be ruined. Instead, new wine belongs in fresh wineskins.”
One Sabbath, Jesus and his disciples were walking through grainfields. As they went, the disciples began picking heads of grain.
The Pharisees said to him, “Look, why are they doing what isn’t allowed on the Sabbath?”
He answered, “Haven’t you ever read what David did when he and his companions were hungry and had nothing to eat?
He went into God’s house during the time Abiathar was high priest and ate the bread set out before God—which only priests are allowed to eat—and he also gave some to his companions.”
Then he said, “The Sabbath was made for people, not people for the Sabbath.
So the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.”
Jesus went into the synagogue again, and there was a man there whose hand was shriveled.
Some people were watching Jesus closely to see if he would heal the man on the Sabbath, so they could accuse him.
Jesus said to the man with the shriveled hand, “Stand up here in front of everyone.”
Then he asked them, “On the Sabbath, is it right to do good or harm, to save a life or take one?” But they didn’t answer.
He looked around at them angrily, deeply grieved by their hard hearts. Then he told the man, “Stretch out your hand.” The man stretched it out, and his hand was restored.
The Pharisees went out and immediately began plotting with the supporters of Herod about how to kill Jesus.
Jesus went with his disciples to the lake. A large crowd followed him from Galilee and Judea,
Jerusalem, Idumea, the region beyond the Jordan, and the areas around Tyre and Sidon. When people heard about everything he was doing, they came to him.
Jesus told his disciples to have a small boat ready for him, so the crowd wouldn’t crush him.
He had healed so many people that everyone with an illness pushed forward to touch him.
Whenever impure spirits saw him, they fell before him and shouted, “You are the Son of God!”
But he strictly ordered them not to reveal who he was.
Jesus went up a mountain and called to himself the people he wanted, and they came to him.
He appointed twelve so they could be with him and so he could send them out to preach,
and gave them authority to drive out demons.
He appointed Simon, whom he named Peter;
James son of Zebedee, and his brother John—he called them Boanerges, meaning “Sons of Thunder”;
Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus, Simon the Zealot,
and Judas Iscariot, who later betrayed him. Then Jesus went into a house.
The crowd gathered again, so that Jesus and his disciples couldn’t even eat.
When his family heard about it, they went to take charge of him, saying, “He’s out of his mind.”
The legal experts who came down from Jerusalem said, “He’s possessed by Beelzebul,” and, “He drives out demons by the ruler of demons.”
Jesus called them over and spoke to them in parables: “How can Satan drive out Satan?
If a kingdom is divided against itself, it can’t stand.
If a household is divided against itself, it can’t stand.
And if Satan has risen up against himself and is divided, he can’t stand; he’s finished.
No one can enter a strong man’s house and steal his things without first tying him up. Then he can rob the house.
I’m telling you the truth: people can be forgiven for every sin and every blasphemy they speak.
But whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will never be forgiven; they’re guilty of an eternal sin.”
He said this because they were claiming, “He has an impure spirit.”
Then Jesus’ mother and brothers arrived. They stayed outside and sent someone in to call him.
A crowd was sitting around him, and they told him, “Your mother, brothers, and sisters are outside looking for you.”
He answered, “Who are my mother and my brothers?”
Then he looked at the people sitting around him and said, “Here are my mother and brothers!
Whoever does God’s will is my brother, sister, and mother.”
Jesus began teaching beside the lake again. A very large crowd gathered around him, so he got into a boat and sat out on the water, while everyone stayed on shore.
He taught them many things through stories. In his teaching he said,
“Listen! A farmer went out to plant seeds.
As he scattered them, some fell along the path, and birds came and ate them up.
Some fell on rocky ground where there wasn’t much soil. They sprouted quickly because the soil wasn’t deep.
But when the sun came up, the plants were scorched. They dried up because they had no roots.
Other seed fell among thornbushes. The thorns grew up and choked it, so it produced no crop.
But some seed fell on good soil. It grew, increased, and produced a crop—some thirty times what was planted, some sixty, and some a hundred.”
Then he said, “Anyone who has ears to hear should listen.”
When Jesus was alone, the people around him, along with the Twelve, asked him about the stories.
He said, “You’ve been given the secret of God’s kingdom. But to those outside, everything is told in stories,
so that ‘they may look and look but not see; they may hear and hear but not understand. Otherwise they might turn back and be forgiven.’”
Then Jesus asked them, “Don’t you understand this story? How will you understand any of the stories?
The farmer plants God’s message.
The seed along the path represents those who hear the message. As soon as they hear it, Satan comes and takes away the message planted in them.
The seed on rocky ground represents those who hear the message and immediately welcome it with joy.
But they have no root and last only a short time. When trouble or persecution comes because of the message, they quickly fall away.
Other seed fell among thornbushes. This represents those who hear the message,
but the worries of this life, the lure of wealth, and desires for other things crowd in and choke the message, so it produces nothing.
The seed in good soil represents those who hear the message, welcome it, and produce a crop—thirty, sixty, or a hundred times what was planted.”
He also said, “Do you bring in a lamp to put it under a basket or a bed? Don’t you put it on a stand?
Whatever is hidden will be brought into the open, and whatever is kept secret will be revealed.
Anyone who has ears to hear should listen.”
He said to them, “Pay attention to what you hear. The measure you use will be measured to you—and even more.
Whoever has will be given more; whoever doesn’t have, even what they have will be taken away.”
He also said, “God’s kingdom is like someone scattering seed on the ground.
Night and day, whether the farmer sleeps or gets up, the seed sprouts and grows, though the farmer doesn’t know how.
The earth produces a crop on its own: first the stalk, then the head, then the full grain in the head.
As soon as the grain is ripe, the farmer puts in the sickle, because harvest time has come.”
He said, “What can we compare God’s kingdom to? What story can we use to explain it?
It’s like a mustard seed, the smallest seed planted in the ground.
But once it’s planted, it grows and becomes the largest garden plant, with branches big enough for the birds to nest in its shade.”
Jesus used many stories like this to share the message with them, as much as they could understand.
He didn’t speak to them without using stories. But when he was alone with his disciples, he explained everything.
That day, when evening came, Jesus said to them, “Let’s cross to the other side.”
They left the crowd and took him with them in the boat, just as he was. Other boats went along too.
A fierce windstorm came up, and waves crashed into the boat until it was filling with water.
Jesus was in the back of the boat, sleeping on a cushion. They woke him and said, “Teacher, don’t you care that we’re going to drown?”
He got up, rebuked the wind, and said to the sea, “Quiet! Be still!” The wind stopped, and everything became calm.
He said to them, “Why are you so afraid? Do you still have no faith?”
They were terrified and said to one another, “Who is this? Even the wind and the sea obey him!”
They crossed the lake and arrived in the region of the Gerasenes.
As soon as Jesus stepped out of the boat, a man with an impure spirit came from the tombs to meet him.
The man lived among the tombs, and no one could restrain him anymore, not even with a chain.
He’d often been bound with shackles and chains, but he tore the chains apart and broke the shackles. No one was strong enough to control him.
Night and day among the tombs and in the hills, he shouted and cut himself with stones.
When he saw Jesus from far away, he ran up and fell on his knees before him.
He shouted, “What do you want with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? Swear by God you won’t torture me!”
For Jesus had already said to him, “Come out of the man, impure spirit!”
Jesus asked him, “What’s your name?” He answered, “My name is Legion, because there are many of us.”
The spirits begged Jesus over and over not to send them out of the region.
A large herd of pigs was feeding on the nearby hillside.
The spirits begged him, “Send us into the pigs. Let us go into them.”
Jesus gave them permission. The impure spirits came out and went into the pigs. The herd—about two thousand—rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned.
The men who had been tending the pigs ran off and reported it in the town and countryside. People came to see what had happened.
When they came to Jesus, they saw the man who’d been controlled by the legion sitting there, dressed and in his right mind, and they were afraid.
Those who had seen it told them what happened to the man and to the pigs.
Then the people began begging Jesus to leave their region.
As Jesus was getting into the boat, the man who’d been demon-possessed begged to go with him.
Jesus wouldn’t let him. Instead he said, “Go home to your family and tell them how much the Lord has done for you and how he’s shown you mercy.”
So the man went away and began telling people in the Ten Cities how much Jesus had done for him. Everyone was amazed.
When Jesus crossed back by boat, a large crowd gathered around him beside the lake.
One of the synagogue leaders, named Jairus, came over. When he saw Jesus, he fell at his feet
and begged earnestly, “My little daughter is dying. Please come and lay your hands on her so she can be healed and live.”
Jesus went with him, and a large crowd followed and pressed around him.
A woman in the crowd had been bleeding for twelve years.
She’d suffered a lot under many doctors, spent all she had, and instead of getting better, she’d grown worse.
When she heard about Jesus, she came up behind him in the crowd and touched his clothes.
She thought, “If I can just touch his clothes, I’ll be healed.”
Immediately her bleeding stopped, and she felt in her body that she was healed from her suffering.
Right away Jesus realized power had gone out from him. He turned around in the crowd and asked, “Who touched my clothes?”
His disciples said, “You see the crowd pressing in on you, and you ask, ‘Who touched me?’”
But Jesus kept looking around to see who had done it.
The woman, trembling with fear because she knew what had happened to her, came and fell at his feet and told him the whole truth.
He said to her, “Daughter, your faith has healed you. Go in peace and be freed from your suffering.”
While Jesus was still speaking, people came from the synagogue leader’s house and said, “Your daughter is dead. Why bother the teacher anymore?”
Jesus heard what they said and told the synagogue leader, “Don’t be afraid. Just believe.”
He didn’t let anyone follow him except Peter, James, and James’ brother John.
When they arrived at the synagogue leader’s home, Jesus saw the commotion, people weeping and wailing loudly.
He went in and said, “Why all this noise and crying? The child isn’t dead; she’s sleeping.”
They laughed at him. But he sent everyone out, took the child’s father and mother and his companions, and went in where the child was.
He took the girl by the hand and said, “Talitha koum!”—which means, “Little girl, I’m telling you, get up!”
Immediately the girl stood up and began walking around. She was twelve years old. They were completely amazed.
Jesus strictly ordered them not to tell anyone what had happened, and told them to give her something to eat.
Jesus left that place and went to his hometown, with his disciples following.
On the Sabbath he began teaching in the synagogue. Many who heard him were amazed. “Where did he get all this?” they asked. “What’s this wisdom he’s been given? How can he do such powerful works?
Isn’t he the carpenter, Mary’s son, and the brother of James, Joses, Judas, and Simon? Aren’t his sisters here with us?” And they took offense at him.
Jesus told them, “A prophet is honored everywhere except in his hometown, among his relatives, and in his own household.”
He couldn’t do any mighty works there, except lay his hands on a few sick people and heal them.
He was amazed at their unbelief. Then he went around the villages teaching.
Jesus called the Twelve and began sending them out two by two. He gave them authority over impure spirits.
He instructed them to take nothing for the journey except a walking stick—no bread, bag, or money in their belts.
They could wear sandals, but weren’t to take an extra shirt.
He said, “Whenever you enter a house, stay there until you leave that place.

If a place won’t welcome you or listen to you, leave and shake the dust off your feet as a warning to them. I’m telling you, it’ll be better for Sodom and Gomorrah on judgment day than for that town.”
So they went out and preached that people should turn back to God.
They drove out many demons, anointed many sick people with oil, and healed them.
King Herod heard about Jesus, because his name had become well known. Some people were saying, “John the Baptist has been raised from the dead, and that’s why these powers are at work in him.”
Others said, “He’s Elijah.” Still others said, “He’s a prophet, like one of the prophets long ago.”
But when Herod heard this, he said, “John, the man I beheaded, has been raised!”
Herod himself had ordered John’s arrest and put him in prison because of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, whom he had married.
John had told Herod, “It’s against the law for you to have your brother’s wife.”
Herodias held a grudge against John and wanted to kill him, but she couldn’t,
because Herod feared John and protected him, knowing he was righteous and holy. Herod was deeply troubled whenever he heard him, yet he liked listening to him.
Then the opportunity came. On his birthday, Herod held a dinner for his officials, military commanders, and leading men of Galilee.
Herodias’ daughter came in and danced, pleasing Herod and his guests. The king told the girl, “Ask me for whatever you want, and I’ll give it to you.”
He swore to her, “I’ll give you whatever you ask, up to half my kingdom.”
She went out and asked her mother, “What should I ask for?” Her mother said, “John the Baptist’s head.”
The girl hurried back to the king and said, “I want you to give me John the Baptist’s head on a platter right now.”
The king was deeply distressed, but because of his promises and his guests, he didn’t want to refuse her.
So he immediately sent an executioner with orders to bring John’s head. The man went and beheaded John in prison,
brought the head on a platter, and gave it to the girl, who gave it to her mother.
When John’s disciples heard what happened, they came, took his body, and laid it in a tomb.
The apostles returned to Jesus and told him everything they’d done and taught.
He said to them, “Come with me by yourselves to a quiet place and get some rest.” So many people were coming and going that they didn’t even have time to eat.
They went away in a boat by themselves to a quiet place.
But many people saw them leave and recognized them. They ran there on foot from all the towns and arrived ahead of them.
When Jesus stepped ashore, he saw a large crowd and felt compassion for them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. So he began teaching them many things.
By now it was late in the day. His disciples came to him and said, “This is a remote place, and it’s getting late.
Send the people away so they can go to the nearby farms and villages and buy something to eat.”
But Jesus answered, “You give them something to eat.” They said, “Should we go and spend two hundred denarii on bread for them?”
He asked, “How many loaves do you have? Go check.” They found out and said, “Five—and two fish.”
Jesus told everyone to sit down in groups on the green grass.
So they sat down in groups of hundreds and fifties.
Jesus took the five loaves and two fish, looked up to heaven, gave thanks, and broke the loaves. He gave them to his disciples to hand out to the people, and he divided the two fish among them all.
Everyone ate and had enough.
The disciples collected twelve baskets full of leftover bread and fish.
Five thousand men had eaten.
Right away Jesus made his disciples get into the boat and go ahead of him to Bethsaida, while he sent the crowd away.
After saying goodbye, he went up the hillside to pray.
When evening came, the boat was out on the lake, and Jesus was alone on land.
He saw them struggling to row because the wind was against them. Around the fourth watch of the night, he came toward them, walking on the lake. He seemed about to pass them by.
When they saw him walking on the lake, they thought he was a ghost and cried out.
They all saw him and were terrified. But he immediately spoke to them: “Take courage! It’s me. Don’t be afraid.”
Then he climbed into the boat with them, and the wind died down. They were completely amazed.
They hadn’t understood what the loaves meant; their hearts were hardened.
They crossed the lake and landed at Gennesaret, where they tied up the boat.
As soon as they got out, people recognized Jesus.
They ran throughout the whole region, carrying sick people on their mats to wherever they heard he was.
Wherever he went—in villages, towns, or countryside—they laid the sick in the marketplaces and begged him to let them touch even the edge of his robe. Everyone who touched him was healed.
The Pharisees and some legal experts who had come from Jerusalem gathered around Jesus.
They noticed that some of his disciples ate with hands considered unclean—that is, without washing them first.
The Pharisees and all the Jews followed the elders’ tradition and wouldn’t eat without carefully washing their hands.
When they came from the marketplace, they wouldn’t eat without washing. They also observed many other traditions, such as washing cups, pitchers, bronze pots, and dining couches.
So the Pharisees and legal experts asked Jesus, “Why don’t your disciples follow the elders’ tradition? They’re eating with unwashed hands!”
He replied, “Isaiah was right when he prophesied about you hypocrites. As Scripture says: ‘These people honor me with their lips, but their hearts are far from me.
Their worship of me is pointless; their teachings are just human rules.’
You let go of God’s command and cling to human traditions—you wash pitchers and cups, and do many similar things.”
Then he said, “You’re very good at setting aside God’s command so you can keep your tradition!
Moses said, ‘Honor your father and mother,’ and, ‘Anyone who curses their father or mother must be put to death.’
But you say that if someone tells their father or mother, ‘Whatever help you might have received from me is Corban’—that is, dedicated to God—
then you no longer let them do anything for their father or mother.
In this way you cancel God’s word through the tradition you’ve passed down. And you do many things like this.”
Jesus called the crowd back and said, “Listen to me, all of you, and understand.
Nothing outside a person that goes into them can make them unclean. What comes out of a person is what makes them unclean.
Anyone who has ears to hear should listen.”
When Jesus went inside away from the crowd, his disciples asked him about the teaching.
He said, “Are you still missing it? Don’t you understand that nothing from outside can make a person unclean
by going into them? It doesn’t enter their heart, but their stomach, and then it goes out of the body.” In saying this, Jesus declared all foods clean.
He continued, “What comes out of a person is what makes them unclean.
For from within, out of people’s hearts, come evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder,
adultery, greed, wickedness, deceit, shamelessness, envy, slander, arrogance, and foolishness.
All these evils come from within and make a person unclean.”
Jesus left that area and went to the region of Tyre. He entered a house and didn’t want anyone to know he was there, but he couldn’t stay hidden.
A woman whose little daughter had an impure spirit heard about him. She came and fell at his feet.
The woman was Greek, born in Syrian Phoenicia, and she begged Jesus to drive the demon out of her daughter.
He said to her, “First let the children eat all they want. It isn’t right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.”
She replied, “Yes, Lord, but even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.”
Then he told her, “Because you said that, you may go. The demon has left your daughter.”
She went home and found her child lying on the bed, with the demon gone.
Jesus left the region of Tyre, traveled through Sidon, and went to the Sea of Galilee and the region of the Decapolis.
Some people brought him a man who was deaf and could barely speak. They begged Jesus to place his hand on him.
Jesus took him away from the crowd, put his fingers in the man’s ears, and touched his tongue with spit.
He looked up to heaven, sighed, and said, “Ephphatha!”—which means, “Be opened!”
At once the man’s ears were opened, his tongue was freed, and he began speaking clearly.
Jesus ordered them not to tell anyone. But the more he ordered them, the more widely they spread the news.
People were completely amazed and said, “He’s done everything well! He even makes deaf people hear and people who can’t speak talk!”
Around that time, a huge crowd had nothing to eat. Jesus called his disciples over and said,
“I feel for these people. They’ve been with me for three days and have nothing to eat.
If I send them home hungry, they’ll collapse on the way. Some of them came a long distance.”
His disciples answered, “Where could anyone get enough bread to feed all these people out here in the wilderness?”
Jesus asked, “How many loaves do you have?” They said, “Seven.”
He told the crowd to sit down. He took the seven loaves, gave thanks, broke them, and handed them to his disciples to distribute. They passed them out to the crowd.
They also had a few small fish. Jesus blessed them and told the disciples to pass those out too.
Everyone ate and was satisfied. The disciples picked up seven baskets of leftovers.
About four thousand people had eaten. Then Jesus sent them home.
Right away, he got into a boat with his disciples and went to the region of Dalmanutha.
The Pharisees came and began arguing with him. They wanted to test him, demanding a sign from heaven.
Jesus sighed deeply and said, “Why does this generation keep demanding a sign? I’m telling you the truth: no sign will be given to this generation.”
Then he left them, got into the boat again, and crossed to the other side.
The disciples had forgotten to bring bread. They had only one loaf with them in the boat.
Jesus warned them, “Watch out! Beware of the yeast of the Pharisees and Herod.”
They discussed this with each other, saying, “He said that because we don’t have bread.”
Jesus knew what they were saying and asked, “Why are you talking about having no bread? Don’t you understand yet? Are your hearts still hard?
You have eyes—can’t you see? You have ears—can’t you hear? Don’t you remember?
When I broke five loaves for the five thousand, how many baskets of leftovers did you collect?” They said, “Twelve.”
“And when I broke seven loaves for the four thousand, how many baskets did you collect?” They said, “Seven.”
He asked them, “Do you still not understand?”
They arrived at Bethsaida. Some people brought a blind man to Jesus and begged him to touch him.
Jesus took the man by the hand and led him outside the village. He spit on the man’s eyes and laid his hands on him, then asked, “Can you see anything?”
The man looked up and said, “I see people, but they look like trees walking around.”
Jesus laid his hands on the man’s eyes again. He looked intently, his sight was restored, and he could see everything clearly.
Jesus sent him home and said, “Don’t go into the village.”
Jesus and his disciples went to the villages around Caesarea Philippi. On the way he asked them, “Who do people say I am?”
They answered, “Some say John the Baptist; others say Elijah; and others say one of the prophets.”
Then Jesus asked them, “But who do you say I am?” Peter replied, “You are the Messiah.”
Jesus warned them not to tell anyone about him.
Then he began teaching them that the Son of Man must suffer many things, be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and legal experts, be killed, and rise again after three days.
He spoke plainly about this. Peter took him aside and began correcting him.
But Jesus turned, looked at his disciples, and rebuked Peter: “Get behind me, Satan! You’re focused on human concerns, not God’s.”
Jesus called the crowd and his disciples over and said, “If anyone wants to follow me, they must say no to themselves, take up their cross, and follow me.
Whoever wants to save their life will lose it, but whoever loses their life for me and the good news will save it.
What good is it for someone to gain the whole world but lose their life?
What could anyone give in exchange for their life?
If anyone is ashamed of me and my words in this unfaithful and sinful generation, the Son of Man will be ashamed of them when he comes in his Father’s glory with the holy angels.”
Jesus said to them, “I’m telling you the truth: some of those standing here won’t die before they see God’s kingdom come with power.”
Six days later, Jesus took Peter, James, and John with him up a high mountain, where they were alone. There he was transformed before them.
His clothes became dazzling white—whiter than anyone on earth could make them.
Elijah and Moses appeared to them, talking with Jesus.
Peter said to Jesus, “Rabbi, it’s good that we’re here. Let’s put up three shelters—one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.”
He didn’t know what to say, because they were terrified.
Then a cloud appeared and covered them, and a voice came from the cloud: “This is my beloved Son. Listen to him!”
Suddenly, when they looked around, they saw no one with them except Jesus.
As they came down the mountain, Jesus ordered them not to tell anyone what they’d seen until the Son of Man had risen from the dead.
They kept this instruction to themselves, but discussed what “rising from the dead” meant.
They asked Jesus, “Why do the legal experts say Elijah must come first?”
He replied, “Elijah does come first to restore everything. But why does Scripture say the Son of Man must suffer greatly and be treated with contempt?
I’m telling you, Elijah has already come, and they did whatever they wanted to him, just as Scripture says.”
When they returned to the other disciples, they saw a large crowd around them and legal experts arguing with them.
As soon as the crowd saw Jesus, they were amazed and ran over to greet him.
He asked, “What are you arguing about with them?”
Someone from the crowd answered, “Teacher, I brought you my son. He has a spirit that takes away his speech.
Whenever it seizes him, it throws him down. He foams at the mouth, grinds his teeth, and becomes stiff. I asked your disciples to drive it out, but they couldn’t.”
Jesus replied, “Unbelieving generation! How long must I stay with you? How long must I put up with you? Bring the boy to me.”
They brought him. As soon as the spirit saw Jesus, it threw the boy into a convulsion. He fell to the ground and rolled around, foaming at the mouth.
Jesus asked the boy’s father, “How long has this been happening?” He said, “Since he was a child.
The spirit has often thrown him into fire or water to kill him. If you can do anything, please take pity on us and help us.”
Jesus said, “If I can? Everything is possible for the one who believes.”
Immediately the father cried out, “I believe! Help me where my faith is weak!”
When Jesus saw the crowd running over, he rebuked the impure spirit: “You deaf and mute spirit, I command you: come out of him and never enter him again!”
The spirit screamed, shook him violently, and came out. The boy looked like a corpse, and many said, “He’s dead.”
But Jesus took him by the hand and lifted him up, and the boy stood.
After Jesus went indoors, his disciples asked him privately, “Why couldn’t we drive it out?”
He told them, “This kind can come out only through prayer.”
They left that place and traveled through Galilee. Jesus didn’t want anyone to know where they were,
because he was teaching his disciples. He told them, “The Son of Man will be handed over to people. They’ll kill him, and after he’s killed, he’ll rise three days later.”
But they didn’t understand what he meant, and they were afraid to ask him.
They came to Capernaum. When they were inside the house, Jesus asked them, “What were you arguing about on the road?”
They didn’t answer, because they’d been arguing about which of them was the greatest.
Jesus sat down, called the Twelve, and said, “If anyone wants to be first, they must be last of all and servant of all.”
He took a little child and stood the child among them. He put his arms around the child and said,
“Whoever welcomes one child like this in my name welcomes me. And whoever welcomes me isn’t welcoming only me, but the one who sent me.”
John said to him, “Teacher, we saw someone driving out demons in your name. We told him to stop, because he wasn’t following us.”
But Jesus said, “Don’t stop him. No one who does a miracle in my name will turn around right away and speak evil of me.
Whoever isn’t against us is for us.
I’m telling you the truth: whoever gives you a cup of water because you belong to Christ will certainly be rewarded.
If anyone causes one of these little ones who believe in me to fall away, it would be better for them to have a large millstone tied around their neck and be thrown into the sea.
If your hand causes you to sin, cut it off. It’s better to enter life crippled than to have two hands and go to hell, into the unquenchable fire.
There the worm doesn’t die, and the fire isn’t put out.
If your foot causes you to sin, cut it off. It’s better to enter life with one foot than to have two feet and be thrown into hell.
There the worm doesn’t die, and the fire isn’t put out.
If your eye causes you to sin, tear it out. It’s better to enter God’s kingdom with one eye than to have two eyes and be thrown into hell,
where the worm doesn’t die and the fire isn’t put out.
Everyone will be salted with fire.
Salt is good, but if it loses its saltiness, how will you make it salty again? Keep salt in yourselves and be at peace with one another.”
Jesus left there and went to the region of Judea and beyond the Jordan. Crowds gathered around him again, and—as he usually did—he taught them.
Some Pharisees came to test him with a question: “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife?”
He answered, “What did Moses command you?”
They said, “Moses allowed a man to write a divorce certificate and send her away.”
Jesus told them, “Moses gave you that command because your hearts were hard.
“But from the beginning of creation, God made them male and female.
“That’s why a man leaves his father and mother and joins his wife,
“and the two become one flesh. They’re no longer two, but one.
“So what God has joined together, no person should separate.”
When they were back in the house, the disciples asked Jesus about it again.
He told them, “Whoever divorces his wife and marries another woman commits adultery against her.
“And if a woman divorces her husband and marries another man, she commits adultery.”
People were bringing little children to Jesus so he could touch them, but the disciples scolded them.
When Jesus saw that, he was upset and told them, “Let the little children come to me! Don’t stop them. God’s Kingdom belongs to people like these.
“I’m telling you the truth: whoever doesn’t welcome God’s Kingdom like a little child will never enter it.”
He took the children in his arms, blessed them, and laid his hands on them.
As Jesus was setting out on the road, a man ran up, knelt before him, and asked, “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?”
Jesus said to him, “Why call me good? No one is good except God alone.
“You know the commandments: ‘Don’t murder. Don’t commit adultery. Don’t steal. Don’t give false testimony. Don’t defraud. Honor your father and mother.’”
The man said, “Teacher, I’ve kept all these since I was young.”

Jesus looked at him with love and said, “There’s one thing you still lack. Go sell what you own and give the money to the poor; then you’ll have treasure in heaven. After that, come follow me, carrying the cross.”
At those words, the man’s face fell. He went away sad, because he had many possessions.
Jesus looked around and told his disciples, “How hard it is for people with wealth to enter God’s Kingdom!”
The disciples were shocked by his words. Jesus said again, “Children, it’s hard to enter God’s Kingdom when you put your trust in wealth.
“It’s easier for a camel to go through a needle’s eye than for a rich person to enter God’s Kingdom.”
They were even more amazed and said to him, “Then who can be saved?”
Jesus looked at them and said, “It’s impossible for people, but not for God. With God, all things are possible.”
Peter began saying to him, “Look, we’ve left everything and followed you.”
Jesus said, “I’m telling you the truth: nobody who has left a house, brothers, sisters, mother, father, children, or land for me and for the good news
“will fail to receive a hundred times as much in this life—houses, brothers, sisters, mothers, children, and land, along with persecution—and eternal life in the age to come.
“But many who are first will be last, and the last will be first.”

They were on the road going up to Jerusalem. Jesus walked ahead of them, and they were amazed; the people following were afraid. He took the twelve aside again and told them what was about to happen to him.
“Look, we’re going up to Jerusalem. The Son of Man will be handed over to the chief priests and legal teachers. They’ll sentence him to death and hand him over to the Gentiles.
“They’ll mock him, spit on him, whip him, and kill him. Then, after three days, he’ll rise again.”
James and John, Zebedee’s sons, came up to Jesus and said, “Teacher, we want you to do whatever we ask.”
He asked them, “What do you want me to do for you?”
They said, “Let one of us sit at your right and the other at your left when you come in glory.”
Jesus told them, “You don’t understand what you’re asking. Can you drink the cup I drink, or be baptized with the baptism I’m baptized with?”
They said, “We can.” Jesus told them, “You will drink the cup I drink and be baptized with the baptism I’m baptized with.
“But sitting at my right or left isn’t mine to grant. Those places belong to the people they’ve been prepared for.”
When the other ten heard about it, they got angry with James and John.
Jesus called them over and said, “You know how rulers of the nations throw their weight around, and their officials boss everyone else.
“It must not be like that among you. Whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant.
“Whoever wants to be first among you must be everyone’s servant.
“Even the Son of Man didn’t come to be served. He came to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many.”
They came to Jericho. As Jesus left with his disciples and a large crowd, Bartimaeus—Timaeus’s son, a blind beggar—was sitting beside the road.
When he heard it was Jesus from Nazareth, he started shouting, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!”
Many people told him to be quiet, but he shouted even louder, “Son of David, have mercy on me!”
Jesus stopped and said, “Call him.” They called the blind man: “Take heart! Get up—he’s calling you!”
Bartimaeus threw off his cloak, jumped up, and went to Jesus.
Jesus asked him, “What do you want me to do for you?” The blind man said, “Rabboni, I want to see again.”
Jesus told him, “Go on your way. Your faith has made you well.” Immediately Bartimaeus could see, and he followed Jesus along the road.
When Jesus and his disciples were near Jerusalem, close to Bethphage and Bethany at the Mount of Olives, he sent two of them ahead
and said, “Go into the village in front of you. As soon as you enter, you’ll find a young donkey tied up, one no one has ever ridden. Untie it and bring it here.
If anyone asks why you’re doing that, say, ‘The Lord needs it and will send it back here soon.’”
They went and found a young donkey tied outside by a doorway in the street. They untied it.
Some people standing there asked, “Why are you untying that young donkey?”
They answered as Jesus had told them, and the people let them go.
They brought the donkey to Jesus, laid their cloaks on it, and he sat on it.
Many people spread their cloaks on the road, while others spread leafy branches they’d cut in the fields.
Those walking ahead of Jesus and those following shouted, “Hosanna! Blessed is the one coming in the Lord’s name!
Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David! Hosanna in the highest heaven!”
Jesus entered Jerusalem and went into the temple. After looking around at everything, he left for Bethany with the Twelve, since it was already late.
The next day, as they were leaving Bethany, Jesus was hungry.
He saw a fig tree in the distance with leaves on it, so he went to see if it had any fruit. But when he reached it, he found only leaves, because it wasn’t fig season.
He said to the tree, “May no one ever eat fruit from you again!” His disciples heard him.
They arrived in Jerusalem. Jesus went into the temple and began driving out the people buying and selling there. He overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves.
He wouldn’t let anyone carry goods through the temple courts.
Then he taught them: “Doesn’t Scripture say, ‘My house will be called a house of prayer for all nations’? But you’ve turned it into a hideout for robbers!”
The chief priests and legal experts heard about this and began looking for a way to kill him. They feared him, because the whole crowd was amazed at his teaching.
When evening came, Jesus and his disciples left the city.
The next morning, as they passed by, they saw the fig tree dried up from the roots.
Peter remembered and said, “Rabbi, look! The fig tree you cursed has dried up.”
Jesus answered, “Have faith in God.
I’m telling you the truth: if anyone says to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and thrown into the sea,’ and doesn’t doubt in their heart but believes it will happen, it will be done.
So I tell you, whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you’ve received it, and it will be yours.
Whenever you stand praying, forgive anyone you have something against, so your Father in heaven may forgive your sins too.
But if you don’t forgive, your Father in heaven won’t forgive your sins either.”
They returned to Jerusalem. As Jesus was walking in the temple courts, the chief priests, legal experts, and elders came to him.
They asked, “By what authority are you doing these things? Who gave you the authority to do them?”
Jesus said, “I’ll ask you one question. Answer me, and I’ll tell you by what authority I do these things.
John’s baptism—was it from heaven or from people? Answer me.”
They discussed it among themselves: “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he’ll ask, ‘Then why didn’t you believe him?’
But if we say, ‘From people’”—they were afraid of the crowd, because everyone believed John was a prophet.
So they answered Jesus, “We don’t know.” Jesus said, “Then I won’t tell you by what authority I do these things.”
Jesus began teaching them through parables: “A man planted a vineyard, put a fence around it, dug a winepress, built a lookout tower, rented it to farmers, and left the country.
When harvest time came, he sent a servant to the farmers to collect his share of the vineyard’s fruit.
They grabbed the servant, beat him, and sent him away with nothing.
The owner sent another servant. They hit him on the head with stones, treated him shamefully, and sent him back.
He sent another, and they killed him. They beat some of the others and killed some too.
The owner still had one person left—his beloved son. At last he sent him, thinking, ‘They’ll respect my son.’
But the farmers said to each other, ‘This is the heir. Come on, let’s kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.’
They grabbed him, killed him, and threw his body out of the vineyard.
“So what will the vineyard owner do? He’ll come, destroy those farmers, and give the vineyard to others.
“Haven’t you read this Scripture? ‘The stone the builders rejected has become the most important cornerstone.
“‘The Lord did this, and it’s amazing to us!’”
The leaders wanted to arrest Jesus, because they knew he’d told the parable against them. But they were afraid of the crowd, so they left him and went away.
Then they sent some Pharisees and supporters of Herod to trap Jesus with his own words.
They came and said, “Teacher, we know you’re honest. You don’t play favorites or try to impress anyone; you teach God’s way truthfully. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar or not?
“Should we pay or shouldn’t we?” Jesus knew their hypocrisy and said, “Why are you testing me? Bring me a denarius; let me see it.”
They brought one. He asked them, “Whose image and inscription are these?” They said, “Caesar’s.”
Jesus said, “Give Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and give God what belongs to God.” They were amazed by him.
Some Sadducees came to Jesus. They say there’s no resurrection. They asked him:
“Teacher, Moses wrote for us: ‘If a man’s brother dies and leaves a wife but no children, his brother must marry the widow and raise children for his brother.’
“There were seven brothers. The first married a woman, then died without leaving any children.
“The second married her, then died without children. The same thing happened to the third.
“All seven married her and died without leaving children. Finally, the woman died too.
“When the dead rise, whose wife will she be? All seven were married to her.”
Jesus answered, “You’ve got it wrong because you don’t know the Scriptures or God’s power.
“When people rise from the dead, they don’t marry or get married. They’re like the angels in heaven.
“And about the dead being raised: haven’t you read in Moses’ book, in the story of the burning bush, how God said, ‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’?
“He isn’t the God of the dead, but of the living. You’re seriously mistaken.”
One of the legal teachers heard them debating and saw that Jesus had answered well. He asked him, “Which commandment is the most important of all?”
Jesus answered, “The most important is: ‘Listen, Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one.
“‘Love the Lord your God with all your heart, all your soul, all your mind, and all your strength.’ That’s the first commandment.
“The second is this: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’ There’s no commandment greater than these.”
The legal teacher said, “Well said, Teacher. You’re right: God is one, and there’s no other.
“And loving God with all your heart, understanding, soul, and strength—and loving your neighbor as yourself—is more important than all burnt offerings and sacrifices.”
When Jesus saw how wisely he answered, he said, “You’re not far from God’s Kingdom.” After that, nobody dared ask him another question.
As Jesus taught in the temple, he asked, “How can the legal teachers say the Christ is David’s son?
“David himself, through the Holy Spirit, said: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand until I put your enemies under your feet.”’
“David himself calls him Lord, so how can the Christ be David’s son?” The large crowd listened to Jesus gladly.
As he taught, Jesus said, “Watch out for the legal teachers. They love walking around in long robes and getting greeted with respect in the marketplaces.
“They want the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at banquets.
“They take over widows’ homes and cover it up with long prayers. They’ll receive a harsher judgment.”
Jesus sat across from the temple treasury and watched people drop money into it. Many rich people put in large amounts.
A poor widow came and dropped in two tiny copper coins, worth a quadrans.
Jesus called his disciples over and said, “I’m telling you the truth: this poor widow put in more than everyone else giving to the treasury.
“They all gave from what they had plenty of, but she, out of her need, gave everything she had—everything she had to live on.”
As Jesus left the temple, one of his disciples said, “Teacher, look at these massive stones and buildings!”
Jesus told him, “You see these huge buildings? Not one stone will stay on top of another. Every one will be thrown down.”
Later, as Jesus sat on the Mount of Olives across from the temple, Peter, James, John, and Andrew asked him privately:
“Tell us, when will this happen? What sign will show that all these things are about to be fulfilled?”
Jesus began answering them: “Watch out. Don’t let anyone lead you off track.
“Many will come using my name, saying, ‘I am he!’ and they’ll lead many people astray.
“When you hear about wars and rumors of wars, don’t panic. These things have to happen, but that isn’t the end yet.
“Nation will fight nation, and kingdom will fight kingdom. There will be earthquakes in different places, famines, and troubles. These are only the first birth pains.
“Keep your eyes open. People will hand you over to councils, beat you in synagogues, and bring you before rulers and kings because of me. Your testimony will reach them.
“But first, the good news must be preached among all nations.
“When they arrest you and hand you over, don’t stress ahead of time about what you’ll say. Say whatever is given to you in that moment, because it won’t be you speaking—it’ll be the Holy Spirit.
“Brothers will hand brothers over to be killed, and fathers will do the same to their children. Children will turn against their parents and have them put to death.
“Everyone will hate you because of my name. But the one who stands firm to the end will be saved.
“When you see the ‘abomination that causes desolation’ standing where it shouldn’t—spoken of by the prophet Daniel; reader, understand this—then those in Judea must run to the mountains.
“If someone’s on the roof, they mustn’t go back inside or come down to grab anything from the house.
“If someone’s out in the field, they mustn’t turn back to get their coat.
“How terrible it will be for pregnant women and mothers nursing babies in those days!
“Pray that you won’t have to flee in winter.
“Those days will bring suffering unlike anything from the beginning of creation, when God made the world, until now—and nothing like it will happen again.
“If the Lord hadn’t shortened those days, nobody would survive. But for the sake of the people he chose, he shortened them.
“If anyone tells you then, ‘Look, here’s the Christ!’ or, ‘Look, he’s over there!’ don’t believe it.
“False Christs and false prophets will show up. They’ll perform signs and wonders to mislead people—even, if possible, the ones God chose.
“Stay alert! I’ve told you everything ahead of time.
“In those days, after that suffering, the sun will go dark, and the moon won’t give its light.
“The stars will fall from the sky, and the powers in heaven will be shaken.
“Then people will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory.
“Then he’ll send out his angels and gather his chosen people from the four winds, from the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven.
“Learn this lesson from the fig tree: when its branch gets tender and its leaves come out, you know summer is near.
“In the same way, when you see these things happening, know that it is near, right at the door.”
“I’m telling you the truth: this generation won’t pass away before all these things happen.
“Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away.
“But nobody knows that day or hour—not the angels in heaven, not even the Son. Only the Father knows.
“Stay alert, keep watch, and pray. You don’t know when the time will come.
“It’s like a man going on a trip. He leaves his house, puts his servants in charge—each with their own work—and tells the doorkeeper to stay awake.
“So stay awake, because you don’t know when the owner of the house is coming: evening, midnight, rooster-crow, or morning.
“Don’t let him arrive suddenly and find you asleep.
“What I’m telling you, I’m telling everyone: stay awake!”
Passover and the Festival of Unleavened Bread were two days away. The chief priests and legal teachers were looking for a sneaky way to arrest Jesus and kill him.
They said, “Not during the festival. The people might riot.”

While Jesus was in Bethany at Simon the leper’s house, he was reclining at the table. A woman came with an alabaster jar of very expensive pure nard perfume. She broke the jar and poured it over his head.
Some people there got angry and said to each other, “Why waste that perfume?
“It could’ve been sold for more than three hundred denarii and given to the poor!” They were harsh with her.
But Jesus said, “Leave her alone. Why are you giving her a hard time? She’s done something good for me.
“You’ll always have the poor with you, and you can help them whenever you want. But you won’t always have me.
“She did what she could. She poured perfume on my body ahead of time to prepare it for burial.
“I’m telling you the truth: wherever the good news is preached throughout the world, people will also remember what she did.”
Then Judas Iscariot, one of the twelve, went to the chief priests to hand Jesus over to them.
They were glad to hear it and promised to pay him. Judas began looking for the right chance to betray Jesus.
On the first day of Unleavened Bread, when the Passover lamb was sacrificed, Jesus’ disciples asked him, “Where should we go prepare the Passover meal for you?”
He sent two disciples and told them, “Go into the city. A man carrying a water jar will meet you. Follow him,
“and wherever he goes in, tell the homeowner, ‘The Teacher asks, “Where’s the guest room where I can eat the Passover with my disciples?”’
“He’ll show you a large upstairs room, furnished and ready. Get everything prepared for us there.”
The disciples went into the city and found everything just as Jesus had told them. They prepared the Passover meal.
That evening, Jesus arrived with the twelve.
As they were reclining at the table and eating, Jesus said, “I’m telling you the truth: one of you will betray me—someone eating with me.”
They were deeply saddened and began asking him one by one, “Surely it isn’t me?”
He answered, “It’s one of the twelve—the one dipping bread with me in the dish.
“The Son of Man goes as Scripture says about him, but how terrible for the one who betrays him! It would have been better for that man if he’d never been born.”
While they were eating, Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to them. “Take it. This is my body.”
Then he took a cup, gave thanks, and passed it to them. They all drank from it.
He said, “This is my blood of the covenant, poured out for many.
“I’m telling you the truth: I won’t drink the fruit of the vine again until that day when I drink it new in God’s Kingdom.”
After they sang a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.
Jesus told them, “All of you will fall away tonight because of me. Scripture says, ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will scatter.’
“But after I’m raised, I’ll go ahead of you to Galilee.”
Peter said, “Even if everybody else falls away, I won’t.”
Jesus told him, “I’m telling you the truth: today—tonight, before the rooster crows twice—you’ll deny me three times.”
But Peter insisted even more, “Even if I have to die with you, I won’t deny you!” And all the others said the same.
They came to a place called Gethsemane. Jesus told his disciples, “Sit here while I pray.”
He took Peter, James, and John with him. He began to feel overwhelmed and deeply distressed.
He told them, “My soul is crushed with sorrow, nearly to death. Stay here and keep watch.”
He went a little farther, fell to the ground, and prayed that, if possible, this hour might pass him by.
He said, “Abba, Father, everything is possible for you. Please take this cup away from me. But not what I want—what you want.”
He came back and found them sleeping. He said to Peter, “Simon, are you asleep? Couldn’t you stay awake for one hour?
“Stay awake and pray so you don’t fall into temptation. The spirit is willing, but the body is weak.”
Jesus went away again and prayed, saying the same words.
When he came back, they were sleeping again; their eyes were so heavy. They didn’t know what to say to him.
He came back a third time and said, “Still sleeping and resting? That’s enough. The hour has come. Look—the Son of Man is being betrayed into the hands of sinners.
“Get up. Let’s go. Look, the one betraying me is here.”
Right away, while Jesus was still speaking, Judas arrived—one of the twelve—with a crowd carrying swords and clubs, sent by the chief priests, legal teachers, and elders.
The betrayer had arranged a signal with them: “The man I kiss is the one. Arrest him and take him away under guard.”
Judas came straight over, saying, “Rabbi! Rabbi!” and kissed him.
Then they grabbed Jesus and arrested him.
One of the people standing there drew a sword, struck the high priest’s servant, and cut off his ear.
Jesus said to them, “Did you come out to arrest me with swords and clubs, like I’m a robber?
“I was right there with you every day in the temple teaching, and you didn’t arrest me. But this is happening so the Scriptures will be fulfilled.”
Then everyone deserted him and ran away.
A young man had been following Jesus, wearing only a linen cloth over his bare body. The young men grabbed him,
but he left the linen cloth behind and ran off naked.
They led Jesus away to the high priest. All the chief priests, elders, and legal teachers gathered there.
Peter followed Jesus from a distance, right into the high priest’s courtyard. He sat with the guards and warmed himself by the fire.
The chief priests and the whole council were looking for testimony against Jesus so they could put him to death, but they couldn’t find any.
Many people gave false testimony against him, but their stories didn’t match.
Some stood up and gave false testimony against him, saying:
“We heard him say, ‘I’ll destroy this temple made by human hands, and in three days I’ll build another one that isn’t made by human hands.’”
But even then, their stories didn’t match.
The high priest stood up in the middle and asked Jesus, “Aren’t you going to answer? What about all these accusations against you?”
But Jesus stayed silent and gave no answer. The high priest asked him again, “Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One?”
Jesus said, “I am. And you’ll see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with heaven’s clouds.”
The high priest tore his clothes and said, “Why do we need any more witnesses?
“You’ve heard the blasphemy! What’s your decision?” They all judged him deserving of death.
Some began spitting on Jesus. They covered his face, hit him with their fists, and said, “Prophesy!” The guards slapped him too.
Peter was down in the courtyard when one of the high priest’s servant girls came by.
She saw Peter warming himself, looked straight at him, and said, “You were with Jesus from Nazareth too!”
But Peter denied it: “I don’t know or understand what you’re talking about.” He went out onto the entryway, and a rooster crowed.
The servant girl saw him and started telling the people standing there, “This man is one of them.”
Peter denied it again. A little later, the people standing nearby said to him, “You’re definitely one of them—you’re a Galilean, and your accent gives you away.”
Peter began cursing and swearing: “I don’t know this man you’re talking about!”
The rooster crowed a second time. Peter remembered Jesus’ words: “Before the rooster crows twice, you’ll deny me three times.” He broke down and wept.
Early that morning, the chief priests met with the elders, legal teachers, and the whole council. They tied Jesus up, took him away, and handed him over to Pilate.
Pilate asked him, “Are you the King of the Jews?” Jesus answered, “That’s what you say.”
The chief priests brought many accusations against him.
Pilate questioned him again: “Aren’t you going to answer? Look at how many charges they’re bringing against you!”
But Jesus gave no further answer, and Pilate was amazed.
At the festival, Pilate usually released one prisoner—the one the people asked for.
There was a man called Barabbas, locked up with fellow rebels who had committed murder during an uprising.
The crowd came forward, shouting and asking Pilate to do what he usually did for them.
Pilate asked them, “Do you want me to release the King of the Jews?”
He knew the chief priests had handed Jesus over because they were jealous.
But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to get Pilate to release Barabbas instead.
Pilate asked them again, “Then what should I do with the man you call the King of the Jews?”
They shouted back, “Crucify him!”
Pilate said, “Why? What has he done wrong?” But they shouted even louder, “Crucify him!”
Pilate wanted to satisfy the crowd, so he released Barabbas. After having Jesus whipped, he handed him over to be crucified.
The soldiers took Jesus into the courtyard—the Praetorium—and called together the whole cohort.
They dressed him in purple, twisted thorn branches into a crown, and placed it on him.
Then they started saluting him: “Hail, King of the Jews!”
They hit his head with a reed, spat on him, and knelt down as if honoring him.
After mocking him, they took off the purple robe and put his own clothes back on him. Then they led him out to crucify him.
A man named Simon of Cyrene, Alexander and Rufus’s father, was coming in from the countryside. They forced him to carry Jesus’ cross.
They brought Jesus to Golgotha, a name that means “Place of a Skull.”
They offered him wine mixed with myrrh, but he wouldn’t drink it.
They crucified him and divided his clothes among themselves, throwing lots to decide who got what.
It was nine in the morning when they crucified him.
The charge against him was written above him: “THE KING OF THE JEWS.”
They crucified two robbers with him, one on his right and one on his left.
This fulfilled the Scripture that says, “He was counted among lawbreakers.”
People passing by insulted him and shook their heads: “Hey! You said you’d destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days.
“Save yourself and come down from the cross!”
The chief priests and legal teachers were mocking him too, saying to each other, “He saved others, but he can’t save himself.
“Let the Christ, Israel’s King, come down from the cross now, so we can see and believe!” Even the people crucified beside him insulted him.
At noon, darkness covered the whole land until three in the afternoon.
At three, Jesus cried out loudly, “Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani?” That means, “My God, my God, why have you abandoned me?”
Some people standing nearby heard him and said, “Look, he’s calling Elijah.”
One person ran, filled a sponge with vinegar, put it on a reed, and offered it to Jesus to drink. He said, “Let’s see whether Elijah comes to take him down.”
Jesus cried out loudly and breathed his last.
The temple curtain ripped in two, from top to bottom.
The centurion standing opposite Jesus saw how he cried out and died. He said, “This man really was the Son of God!”
Some women were watching from a distance. Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the younger and Joses, and Salome.
They had followed Jesus and cared for him when he was in Galilee. Many other women had also come with him to Jerusalem.
By evening, since it was Preparation Day—the day before the Sabbath—
Joseph of Arimathaea arrived. He was a respected council member who was also waiting for God’s Kingdom. He boldly went to Pilate and asked for Jesus’ body.
Pilate was surprised Jesus had already died. He called the centurion over and asked whether Jesus had been dead for a while.
After getting confirmation from the centurion, Pilate gave the body to Joseph.
Joseph bought a linen cloth, took Jesus down, wrapped him in it, and laid him in a tomb cut into rock. Then he rolled a stone across the tomb’s entrance.
Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses saw where Jesus was laid.
After the Sabbath, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices so they could go and anoint Jesus’ body.
Very early on the first day of the week, just after sunrise, they went to the tomb.
They were asking one another, “Who will roll the stone away from the entrance for us?”
But when they looked up, they saw that the very large stone had already been rolled away.
They entered the tomb and saw a young man sitting on the right side, wearing a white robe. They were alarmed.
He said, “Don’t be alarmed. You’re looking for Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has risen! He isn’t here. Look, this is where they laid him.
Now go tell his disciples and Peter, ‘He’s going ahead of you into Galilee. You’ll see him there, just as he told you.’”
They went out and ran from the tomb, trembling and overwhelmed. They didn’t say anything to anyone, because they were afraid.
After Jesus rose early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, the woman from whom he had driven out seven demons.
She went and told the people who had been with him, while they were mourning and crying.
When they heard that Jesus was alive and that she’d seen him, they didn’t believe her.
After that, Jesus appeared in a different form to two of them as they were walking into the countryside.
They went back and told the others, but the others didn’t believe them either.
Later Jesus appeared to the Eleven while they were eating. He rebuked them for their unbelief and stubbornness, because they hadn’t believed the people who saw him after he was raised.
He told them, “Go throughout the whole world and announce the good news to everyone.
Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever refuses to believe will be condemned.
These signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they’ll drive out demons, and they’ll speak in new languages.
They’ll pick up snakes, and if they drink anything poisonous, it won’t hurt them. They’ll place their hands on the sick, and the sick will recover.”
After the Lord Jesus had spoken to them, he was taken up into heaven and sat down at God’s right hand.
The disciples went out and preached everywhere. The Lord worked with them and confirmed the message through the signs that accompanied it. Amen.
